headline: Your mouth is the counter. Your denture is the cutting board.
alt_hooks:
Four rounds of thrush medicine.

Every one worked.

Every one failed three weeks later.

I found out why from the man who used to inspect my kitchen.

Hold a flashlight to the roof of your mouth tonight.

If the red patch is shaped exactly like your denture, keep reading.

Mine was. And no doctor had told me what that meant.
script:
I cooked for a living for thirty-one years.

Last March, I salted my own gravy four times.

I still couldn't taste it.

And the roof of my mouth burned like I'd gulped hot coffee. Every single day.

Something was living in my teeth. And every doctor kept treating the wrong thing.

Let me back up.

My name is Marlene. I'm seventy-one. I live in Spokane, Washington.

I ran the line at a family diner. Pot roast Sundays. Pies on Thursdays.

I've worn a full upper plate since I was fifty-eight.

Here's what last winter took from me.

I quit making Sunday supper. What's the point if you can't taste it?

I skipped the church potluck. I couldn't tell if my own scalloped potatoes were any good.

My granddaughter Shayla asked me to teach her my pie crust. I kept saying next month.

My doctor took one look. Thrush. Nystatin rinse. Twenty-two dollars.

It cleared in ten days.

Three weeks later, it was back.

Then fluconazole pills. Then a stronger rinse.

Every time it cleared.

Every time it came back.

And I did everything right with the teeth. Polident every morning. Efferdent at night. A stiff brush. A thirty-dollar pod off Amazon that hummed and did nothing.

Rock bottom was Shayla's sixteenth birthday.

I made her lemon meringue.

I tasted it in the kitchen. Wet paper. And it stung.

I shut myself in the pantry and cried into a dish towel.

The person who figured it out wasn't a doctor.

It was Gene. The retired county inspector who used to walk my kitchen with a clipboard. I ran into him at the pharmacy, picking up round four.

"Marlene. What are you doing about the plate?"

You know an old wooden cutting board? Full of knife scratches?

Scrub the counter all day. Put that same board back down, and the counter's dirty again.

Your mouth is the counter. Your denture is the cutting board.

It has a name. Denture stomatitis. Candida yeast, living in the tiny pores of the acrylic.

Up to two-thirds of denture wearers get it.

The pills clear your mouth. Then the plate goes back in and seeds the yeast right back.

You're treating the mouth. Not the denture.

Polident fizzed on the surface. That stiff brush carved new scratches for it to hide in.

Try this tonight.

Take your plate out. Shine a flashlight on the roof of your mouth.

If the red stops exactly where the plate stops, it isn't your mouth.

Mine was a perfect outline.

So I wrote a list, like a recipe.

Reach into the pores.

Kill what shakes loose.

No chemicals against my palate.

Five minutes, or I'd quit.

And proof.

Gene sent me a ninety-day lab test. Seven leading ultrasonic cleaners. One came out on top.

The DentalPULSE Pod.

The other six left live bacteria. Like my thirty-dollar pod that hummed.

This one shakes the plate clean forty-two thousand times a second, then hits it with medical-grade UV-C light. Tap water. One button.

I almost didn't open the box. I'd been fooled once already.

First morning, five minutes later, the water was cloudy. Little brown specks floating in it.

That had been in my mouth. After Polident. After brushing.

Week one, the burning eased.

Week two, my coffee stopped stinging.

Week three, the red outline was gone. My doctor said, whatever you're doing, keep doing it.

Week five, I tasted salt.

I cried again. Different reason.

Sunday supper is back. Six chairs.

My scalloped potatoes went to the potluck. The pan came home empty.

Shayla learned my pie crust. She made her own lemon meringue. I tasted every bite.

My sister Faye wears a lower partial. She bought one the same week.

And last Sunday I salted the gravy once.

It was perfect.

The yeast was never in my mouth. It was living in my teeth.

headline: She was counting my bites. I didn't know why I'd stopped eating.

My doctor said dry mouth.

My dentist said thrush, three times.

A retired microbiologist on my old mail route looked for five seconds and said, "Arnie, you're treating the mouth, not the denture."

For sixteen years, my wife never saw me without my teeth.

That was the problem.

I found out the night she put a notebook on the kitchen table and asked if I was dying.
script:
I found my wife's notebook in the junk drawer.

Every page was about me.

Tuesday. Four bites of meatloaf. Wednesday. Half a pancake. Thursday. Soup. Didn't finish.

She'd been counting my bites for two months.

I'd lost nineteen pounds and told nobody why.

By the end, you'll know what was really in my mouth. And what she wrote on the last page.

Let me back up.

I slept in them, too. Arlene never saw me without my teeth.

Two winters ago, the roof of my mouth started burning. Like a pizza burn that never healed.

Then everything tasted like pennies. Coffee. Pork chops. Arlene's apple cake.

First morning, the water came out cloudy and brown.

That had been sitting on the roof of my mouth for years.

I started taking them out at night. Arlene saw me without teeth for the first time in sixteen years. She laughed till she cried.

Week one, the burning backed off.

Week three, coffee tasted like coffee.

Week six, the red outline was gone. My dentist said, whatever you're doing, keep doing it.

I'm back at the Legion on Fridays. Two pieces of walleye. Tyler came along last week.

Nine pounds back on.

Sunday. Two pork chops. Apple cake. Seconds.

headline: It wasn't an allergy. It was living in my plate.
alt_hooks:
"You'd never comb a client with a dirty comb."

"So why have you been putting one in your mouth every morning for six years?"

That's what my client said, right before I tore up a two thousand dollar check.

Two thousand one hundred dollars.

That's what I almost paid to fix an allergy I never had.

The real cause was something every new set of teeth would have caught too.
script:
I had the check written.

Two thousand one hundred dollars.

For a whole new set of teeth.

My dentist said I was probably allergic to my denture.

I believed him.

Then a client saw that check and said, "Don't you dare."

She was right.

What she told me still makes my skin crawl.

Let me back up.

I'm Bonnie. I'm sixty-three. I've owned a two-chair salon in Savannah, Georgia, for twenty-six years.

I've worn an upper plate for six.

Last summer the roof of my mouth turned red. Angry red.

It burned like a whole bag of salt and vinegar chips. Sweet tea stung.

Here's what it took.

I quit talking with my clients. Twenty-six years of gossip, and I went quiet. Talking made it burn.

I skipped my sister's crab boil on Tybee.

And I stopped kissing my husband, Dale. I told him I had a sore.

That was half true.

My doctor said thrush. Nystatin. It cleared.

It came back.

Fluconazole. Cleared.

Came back.

Over a hundred dollars in prescriptions. I tried Polident, then Efferdent. Brushed it twice a day.

Then my dentist said the word allergy. Maybe the acrylic itself.

New set. Two thousand one hundred dollars.

I wrote the check, then sat in my car and cried.

That Thursday, Miss Yvonne sat in my chair. Every other Thursday for eleven years.

She's made dentures in a dental lab for thirty years. She saw the check on my station.

"Bonnie. A true acrylic allergy is rare. What you've got is yeast. And it's living in that plate."

"You'd never comb a client with a dirty comb. Every comb goes in the blue jar."

"Honey, you've been putting the same dirty comb in your mouth every morning for six years."

It's called denture stomatitis. Candida yeast, living in the tiny pores of the acrylic.

Up to two-thirds of denture wearers get it.

The pills clean your mouth. You put the plate back in. The yeast reseeds.

Treating the mouth. Not the denture.

A new set? Clean it the same way and the yeast moves right in. Two thousand dollars later.

And the allergy?

Back in 2008, the FDA warned about allergic reactions to persulfate. That's in a lot of denture tablets.

If anything was an allergy, it was what I soaked my teeth in.

She gave me a test.

After cleaning, run a fingernail along the inside of your plate.

White paste? That's been sitting on your palate all day.

I did it right there. A white line under my nail.

I tore up the check.

I needed four things.

Ninety-nine ninety-five. Not two thousand one hundred.

I still almost sent it back unopened. I'd been let down too many times.

The first cycle, the water went cloudy. Brownish.

I'd brushed that plate an hour before.

I made Dale come look. He said, "That was in your mouth?"

From then on, the plate came out every night.

Week one, the burning eased.

Week three, sweet tea stopped stinging.

Week five, the red was gone. My dentist looked twice. "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it."

I'm talking in the salon again. Too much, Dale says.

I made the next crab boil. Ate my weight in shrimp.

And Dale got his kisses back.

Miss Yvonne still sits in my chair every other Thursday. Now she checks my plate before I check her roots.
